newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fate of Singapore opposition leader still unclear.
newsitem.headline: Fate of Singapore opposition leader still unclear.

text.p: The fate of prominent Singapore opposition figure Chee Soon Juan remained unclear on Friday after a marathon parliamentary hearing over charges of contempt against him and three of his colleagues.

Chee, the secretary-general of the opposition Singapore Democratic Party, and the other SDP members faced 12 hours of questioning among them on Thursday on allegations they had deliberately misled a parliamentary select committee in August.
If found guilty by parliament, Chee and the others could be fined up to Singapore $50,000 (US$35,460) each or jailed.

Parliament could decide to refer the matter to the attorney-general for possible prosecution. If they were then convicted in the courts and sentenced beyond certain minimum fines or jail terms, they could be barred from contesting future elections.

The Clerk of Parliament told Reuters on Friday that the proceedings of the Committee of Privileges, which is considering the case, had not ended and the accused could be recalled before final deliberations.

"Even though the four witnesses have been released for the time being, they can be recalled to give further evidence," P.O. Ram said. He said a date had yet to be fixed for the committee to give its decision.
Chee has the highest profile in the SDP and is widely expected to run for parliament in the next election, which is due by April 1997.

The opposition won just four of 81 parliamentary seats in the last general election in 1991. The SDP took three of the four and gained an average of between 48 and 49 percent of the vote in the handful of seats it contested.
The hearing was called after a complaint by Health Minister George Yeo that the SDP lied to a Select Committee on health.

An SDP document submitted to the committee in August had claimed government spending on healthcare had fallen to only five percent of total expenditure in the 1990s from around 40 percent 20 years earlier.
The figure for the 1990s was incorrect and should have been 25.4 percent, the SDP later said.

Chee and his colleages -- Wong Hong Toy, S. Kunalen and Kwan Yue Keng -- have denied charges of perjury, prevarication, misconduct and wilfully giving false evidence, saying the figure was a typing mistake and a result of human error.
